turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Friday, the thirtieth of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Christine Lagarde is leaving the European Central Bank nine months early. She announced it hours after holding interest rates.
[thoughtful] Nine months.
And her reason was not the economy. It was that she could no longer be neutral.
Second — a Swedish company sells the best gloves in the world, and its own product feed says the good ones are made in Hungary.
Which turns out to be the shape of the whole day.
[amused] And third, Sri Lanka has taken a million families off its welfare roll, and the monthly payment went up.
Start in Frankfurt. Thursday afternoon. The Governing Council holds the deposit rate at two point five per cent — unanimously.
With inflation at what?
Three point eight per cent. Nearly double their target. Energy up eighteen point nine per cent on the year.
[curious] And they held anyway.
She said conditions could have warranted tightening. Markets price roughly three more increases by the end of twenty twenty-seven.
So why leave?
Her words. Quote — I don't think that I can remain neutral. I don't think that I can be comfortable in that neutrality at the present time.
[pause] That's a strange thing for a central banker to say.
It is the most interesting thing anyone said this week.
Is she going somewhere?
Nobody has confirmed anything. What is confirmed is the date — the seventh of February, twenty twenty-seven.
Okay. Here's my question. Who picks the next one?

Not the bank. The European Council. Heads of government. Isabel Schnabel goes in early January. The chief economist, Philip Lane, in May. Two more Executive Board seats open in the first half of twenty twenty-seven. Four of six. One analyst expects them filled as a package, no later than the December summit.
[skeptical] And the French election is in April.
Which is exactly what both sides of French politics said out loud. The far left and the far right made the same accusation on the same afternoon.
The same accusation?
That the president is locking in the appointment before he can lose it.
Huh. What did the economists say?
Paul De Grauwe at the London School of Economics — this is debasing the institution and just following the purely political calculus of the French President.
[exhales] Strong.
A German member of the European Parliament said a departure timed around a national election damages trust in an institution that must stand above domestic political calculation.
And the other side?

Marcel Fratzscher at the Berlin institute called it a strong sense of responsibility towards Europe. Goldman's fixed-income deputy said institutional behaviour outlasts any one president. The market shrugged. The euro fell two tenths of a per cent. The Guardian's write-up reached Hacker News and got five points and no comments.
[laughs] Five points. For the end of an era.

One number she leaves behind. France pays a hundred and fifty-five basis points more than Germany to borrow for ten years. A decades high. That's the inheritance. Now — Washington, because the same shape turns up. Wednesday. The Federal Open Market Committee holds its range at three and three quarters to four per cent. Ten votes to two.
And the two?
Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack. Both wanted to raise.
[curious] Dissenting in the hawkish direction. That's unusual.
The statement ends with a sentence I haven't seen before. Quote — The Committee will deliver price stability. No. And here's the part almost nobody reads. The implementation note.
The what?
The technical instruction that goes out with the decision. It tells the trading desk, when appropriate, to increase the System Open Market Account through purchases of Treasury bills.
[pause] Wait. They're buying?
They're buying. And reinvesting agency principal into bills. To maintain, quote, ample reserves.
So the price of money is restrictive and the quantity is going up.
That is exactly it. The headline says hold. The desk says add.
Mm. That's the label and the hands again.

Then Thursday morning the data arrived, all at once. Growth in the third quarter, three point four per cent annualised, up from two point two. And September's inflation gauge — three point six per cent on the year, up from three point four. Core at three point one. Here's the whiplash. On the twenty-sixth of October the market priced another increase at below ten per cent. Three days later it was above eighty.
[gasps] From ten to eighty?
In three days. Nobody owns this call.
What's actually driving the inflation?

Oil. Brent settled at a hundred and fifteen dollars and thirty-two cents, up about eighteen per cent on the month and eighty on the year, after attacks on shipping near Hormuz. American inflation at three point six. Euro area three point eight. Australia four point three. Three central banks, one price.
What does that do to a normal portfolio?
It breaks the hedge. Equities and bonds are both priced off the same oil-driven variable, so they fall together. Bonds hedge a slowdown. They do not hedge a shortage.
And gold?

Gold fell three point three per cent on the month — while its opportunity cost was falling. The safe-haven money went into Treasuries instead. Central banks bought thirty-nine tonnes in August, which is the floor under it. And bitcoin is trading as a high-beta technology expression, not as a liquidity asset. Market explanation, not advice. Never a buy or sell call on this desk. The Housing Board published revised plans on Wednesday for Maju Forest and Gillman Barracks. Twelve hundred fewer homes than the July plan.
Why fewer?
To keep trees. Retention at Maju Forest goes from about eight hectares to ten, of a twenty-three hectare site. At Gillman, eight to twelve.
How much feedback did they get?

Nine thousand five hundred submissions. Seven thousand two hundred on Maju Forest alone. Twelve hundred homes for about four hectares. The Bird Society called it a good compromise. A Nature Society member said keeping ten hectares beats clearing two-thirds of it.
Anyone unhappy?
A Sunset Way resident of five decades, who says her residents' group was not invited to the options session held with the nature groups.
[thoughtful] So the consultation had a guest list.

The second Singapore decision has more teeth. The Monetary Authority told banks to act on haze findings — engage customers linked to fires, and escalate as far as exiting the relationship. Clear breaches of environmental laws would warrant stronger measures, in their words.
And the law behind it?
Twelve years old. Zero prosecutions. A hundred thousand dollars a day in penalties that nobody has ever collected.
[sighs] Right.
Now chips, and this is the one that made me laugh.
[curious] Go.

Samsung reported its results on Thursday. Operating profit a hundred and seven point four trillion won. An all-time high. A hundred and six point five trillion of it came from the chip division. That's ninety-nine point one per cent of the group.
[pause] Ninety-nine?
And the division that makes the phones and the televisions posted an operating loss of eight hundred billion won. Because it's buying memory. From itself.
[laughs] That's absurd. That's genuinely absurd.

SK hynix the day before. Revenue above a hundred trillion won for the first time. Operating margin, eighty per cent. And it says demand will exceed supply through twenty thirty, with fourteen customers already contracted for more than half of its twenty twenty-seven capacity.
Who's paying for all this?
Alphabet. Capital spending of fifty-one point four billion dollars in the quarter, against twenty-four a year earlier.
And the cash flow?
Minus nine point zero seven billion. Negative.
[gasps] Free cash flow went negative at Alphabet.
Microsoft spent thirty-nine point four billion in the same quarter. Neither raised its forecast.
So the buyers crossed zero and the sellers are at eighty per cent margin. Is anybody pushing back on the shortage story?

Acer's chief executive says the memory makers are hyping it to protect margins, and expects PC prices to fall by late twenty twenty-seven. Entirely checkable. And on the forums the shortage is personal. One user: I would love to build a home language-model server, but ten thousand is not in my budget right now.
[chuckles] Been there.

Another: I have ninety-six gigabytes of good memory, bought three years ago, up around five hundred and fifty per cent. If a stick dies, it dies. Very sad. Speaking of which — Mistral released the weights for its biggest model on Thursday. Free. About a trillion parameters. The smallest usable build anyone has published is two hundred and thirty-three gigabytes.
And to run that?
Two hundred and fifty-six gigabytes of memory. A top-end Mac Studio, or two of Nvidia's little desktop boxes.
[laughs] So it's free the way a yacht is free if someone gives you a yacht.
One man on Hacker News got very close. His line was — Ugh, okay, that's out of my league. Almost though. Another thirty-two gigabytes and it would work.
[warmly] Thirty-two gigabytes short. That's painful.
The quantiser published the fidelity curve, which almost nobody does. Divergence falls forty-fold from one bit to six, while the file size rises less than fourfold.
So most of the quality is cheap.

Almost all of it is bought in the first three hundred and seventy gigabytes. Apple put touch on the MacBook Pro. Announced Wednesday. Pre-orders open here today. Three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine Singapore dollars for the fourteen-inch.
And the non-touch one? So a thousand dollars for touch.
A thousand dollars for the panel, the touch layer, and about two hundred and twenty grams. The processor is the same chip Apple shipped in March.
[deadpan] A thousand dollars for a subtraction of weight.
The display is genuinely good — two thousand nits for both bright and standard content, ten million to one contrast.
What's the funny number?
The most expensive configuration anybody built is fourteen thousand five hundred and forty-nine dollars, mostly a seven-thousand-dollar storage option.
[laughs] Okay.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this. [excited] Oh, I like this one already.
In September twenty eighteen a pilot called James Payne took a sailplane to twenty-two thousand six hundred and fifty-seven metres over Argentina. Without an engine. In a mountain wave.
How does that even work?
A glider is always sinking through the air around it, at about half a metre a second. The art is finding air going up faster than that.
And there are different kinds?

Four. Thermals, off warm ground. Ridge lift, wind pushed up a hillside — needs twenty to twenty-five knots. Wave, the standing oscillation downwind of mountains. And convergence, where two air masses meet.
What's the measure of a good glider?

Glide ratio. A German research group measured one modern eighteen-metre machine at about fifty-seven to one. Competition pilots average around a hundred and twenty kilometres an hour over tasks up to a thousand kilometres.
So what does it cost?
[wry] That is the finding. Not one European sailplane factory publishes a price.
Not one?
Not one. Six manufacturers, every single one routes you to a quote form or a sales email. Every price circulating online is a decade old or an aggregator's invention.
[scoffs] That's a choice.
A used classic single-seater runs twenty to forty-five thousand US dollars. A new-ish eighteen-metre racer, a hundred and ninety-nine thousand.
And the instruments? You know I want the instruments.
A full panel is about ten thousand one hundred and eighty dollars before a transponder. The flagship vario alone is two thousand three hundred and ninety.
What does a vario do?

Tells you whether the air you're in is going up. The current one has an eight-g accelerometer, three gyros, a thermal assistant that combines seven analysis methods, and it says HEAD ON out loud if something is coming at you.
[laughs] It shouts at you.
And the best glide computer software is free and open source. It even reads telemetry from the simulator, so you can practise at home with the real instrument.
Okay, now the honest bit. Why is the sport shrinking?

One association in Victoria put it in a sentence, and it's the best line in the issue. Quote — the loss of one hundred members over eight years cannot be solved through recruitment alone. If a hundred people are recruited but a similar number leave, the organisation remains at the same level.
[thoughtful] Recruitment is not retention.
Their membership went from six hundred and sixty-seven to five hundred and sixty-seven in eight years. Women are eleven point eight per cent of members and twenty-eight per cent of trial flights.
So the funnel works and the bucket leaks.

And here's why flying is cheap at all. A pilot on an old mailing list: it is due to the subsidy of free unskilled and skilled labour, provided by club members gratis. Membership at one Australian club is five hundred and ninety-five dollars if you volunteer and one thousand one hundred and ninety if you don't.
[laughs] They've literally priced it.
Instruction is free. Against powered flying at over a hundred and fifty pounds an hour.
Can you do this from Singapore?
No. There is no gliding in Singapore, and the desk found no active full-size club in Malaysia either.
So where?
Australia. A seven-day beginner's course at Benalla is three thousand eight hundred and fifty Australian dollars, including about thirty tows, membership, a logbook and a bucket hat.
[amused] The hat is itemised.
Some students go solo inside the week. And before you spend anything — the simulator licence is a hundred and twenty US dollars.
Is it dangerous?
Here are the real numbers. Europe recorded ten fatal accidents and twelve deaths in twenty twenty-four — the lowest the regulator has ever logged.
And America?

Twenty-one accidents in the year to October twenty twenty-four. Two fatal. And the breakdown surprised me — ten of the twenty-one happened while landing, and six of those at an airport, not in a field. Not the farmer's field. But the five launch accidents produced both deaths. Since twenty twenty-one, no fatal accident has happened in the cruise.
So the dangerous parts are the start and the finish.
And the safety foundation admits it cannot get flight-hour data — the community has been unable or unwilling to reliably submit flight hours.
[sighs] They can't count themselves either.
Which brings us back. Two more quickly. The Atelier did leather gloves. Every online shop publishes a machine-readable product feed. The Swedish maker's feed names its suppliers.
And?
Eight hundred and eighty-one products. Sixteen suppliers. Three hundred and twenty from Vietnam, two hundred and twenty-nine from China, sixty-seven from its own Hungarian factory.
And the expensive ones?
All eight of the hand-cut peccary and carpincho pairs — the five hundred and twenty-five to six hundred and twenty-five dollar tier — are attributed to a Hungarian co-operative.
What does the Swedish supplier make?
[deadpan] The leather balm.
[laughs] Of course it does.
Nobody is lying. The name is honest about everything except where the hands are.
What should a buyer actually look for?
Three things. A quirk — a little triangular insert at the base of a finger. The seam type. And peccary's bristle follicles come in groups of three. The grain is the certificate.
And what does the money buy?
Hours. One house says thirty-two stages and up to eight hours a glove. A machine-sewn pair takes under thirty minutes. One seamstress finishes about two and a half pairs a day.
[thoughtful] Two and a half pairs. All day.
And one honest number for anyone in Singapore — nobody here needs a lined glove. This is a travel category.
Culture, quickly?
A documentary about Elizabeth Holmes grew twenty-five per cent in its second weekend. To nineteen and a half million dollars.
Grew? Second weekends go down.

It tripled its cinema count and the per-screen average still beat the number-one film. Ninety-seven per cent from a hundred and ninety-five critics. The audience panel is noisier — twenty-three negative ratings out of two hundred and thirty-one. And we printed a correction today on a film we scored mid-count a week ago.
[warmly] Good. Say it when you get it wrong.

Family desk, one finding, and it matters if you have a twelve-year-old. Eleven thousand two hundred and seventy-nine children, five annual waves. Problem social-media use and depression do feed each other — but not at twelve.
When?
From thirteen. At twelve to thirteen the effect is statistically nothing. At thirteen to fourteen it appears, and at fourteen to fifteen it's strongest.
And anxiety?
Nothing. All eight anxiety paths, across five years, non-significant. One wrinkle worth noticing. The social-media score was filled in by the child. The depression score was filled in by the parent.
[pause] Different hands again.
And on rules — strict household screen rules buy about fifty-six minutes a day. The gain erodes by thirteen minutes for every year the child gets older.
And parents give up?
Measurably. The strictest group went from forty-six point nine per cent of families to twenty-five point three in two years.
What's the one rule that works?
Not a time limit. The strongest predictor by far is a device playing in the room as the child falls asleep. It costs nothing to fix.
[warmly] That's the actionable one.
Fitness, one line. A UK Biobank curve found cardiorespiratory fitness keeps reducing mortality risk with no plateau at all — while grip strength stops paying at the median.
So grip is a floor test.

Grip is a floor test. Fitness is a ladder. General guidance, not medical advice. Sri Lanka. [pause] A programme called Aswesuma — the word means solace. It replaced an older scheme in twenty twenty-three. In twenty twenty-five it paid two million four hundred and thirty-nine thousand families. By August it paid one million two hundred and fifty-one thousand.
So over a million families came off. And the money saved?
None. In November the scheme paid eleven point two billion rupees. In July, eleven point eight three billion.
[pause] It went up.
The rates were raised in the same breath that the roll was cut. Paying more, to fewer.
Who ordered this?

Everybody says the International Monetary Fund. And the Fund's binding condition is a floor on social spending measured in rupees — not in households. So a government can pass every quarterly review while removing a million families, provided it pays more to the ones who stay. The austerity is invisible in the fiscal numbers.
And the written condition?
To obtain cabinet approval of an updated graduation strategy. That's it. The report does not require removing any tier.
[thoughtful] So the label says Washington.
And the hands are in Colombo. A minister in the governing party told a public meeting that recipients should be ashamed, and that the payment is like begging legally.
[exhales] That's a government elected against austerity.
A local writer answered him — social welfare is not begging, it is the mark of a caring and civilised society.
Does the targeting even work?

A quarter of recipients are not poor. And fifty-eight per cent of poor households get nothing — which is worse than the scheme it replaced. Some are. That's the honest part. But Brazil ran the same exercise with the same technology and added two point nine million families while removing three point four.
The same machine, used as a valve instead of a gate.
Brazil's tiers have no expiry date. Sri Lanka's do.
[thoughtful] And nobody outside has written this up.
Not the Times, not the BBC, not Reuters, not the FT, not the Economist. We checked all five.
What ties the book together today?
A Swedish glove cut in Hungary. A central bank whose successor is chosen by prime ministers. A committee that holds the rate while its own desk buys bills.
A child's answers and a parent's answers, added up as one finding.
A sport that flies on donated labour. And a welfare cut whose only written instruction says nothing of the kind.
The label and the hands.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
